legend: Physiological regulation of proliferation and aldosterone production is intimately coupled to depolarization of the membrane potential in the zona glomerulosa (left). Mutations in various membrane-bound ion channels (right) mimic the stimulatory role of angiotensin II, causing depolarization either through the increased influx of sodium (mutant KCNJ5) or calcium (mutant CACNA1H/CACNA1D), or through the inhibition of extracellular transportation of sodium (mutant ATP1A1) or calcium (mutant ATP2B3), or through the increased efflux of chloride ions (mutant CLCN2).

legend: The PKA signalling pathway mediates the zona fasciculata response to ACTH binding the ACTH receptor (MC2R) and activating adenylyl cyclase (AC). The increasing levels of cAMP will release the inhibition of the catalytic PKA subunits (PKA-C) by the regulatory PKA subunit (PKA-R), stimulating cell growth and cortisol production. Aberrant PKA signalling is a recurrent theme in cortisol-secreting adrenal cortical lesions and might stem from activating mutations (green stars) as well as inactivating events (pink stars). GPCR, G protein–coupled receptor; PDE, phosphodiesterase.

legend: Adrenal cortical adenomas can show cystic, haemorrhagic, and degenerative features, which should not be misinterpreted as necrosis or as a vascular neoplasm.
Adrenal cortical adenoma can show myelolipomatous change. This feature is not known to be of clinical significance.
Myxoid change can be seen in adrenal cortical neoplasms. The biological potential of myxoid adrenal cortical neoplasms may be difficult to predict with standard Weiss criteria.

This virilizing adrenal cortical adenoma is composed of sheets of cells with compact eosinophilic cytoplasm. Virilizing adrenal tumours are more common in children, whereas feminizing tumours are more common in adults.
Cushing syndrome–associated adrenal cortical adenomas are usually composed of predominantly pale-staining, lipid-rich, zona fasciculata–like cells, but they can have variable cell types.

Cortisol-secreting adrenal cortical adenomas are often composed of zona fasciculata–like cells with markedly vacuolated cytoplasm, giving the lesion a clear appearance at low magnification. These lesions often have a nesting pattern of growth, or they may have trabeculae, cords of cells, or mixtures of cell types. The predominance of lipid-rich cells gives the tumour a yellow appearance on cut section grossly.
Adrenal cortical adenomas with primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) are not associated with atrophy of the associated adrenal cortex, as is seen in cortisol-producing adrenal cortical adenomas.

Aldosterone-secreting adrenal cortical adenomas have a predominantly nesting or alveolar pattern of growth. Lipid-rich, pale-staining cells are often identified in the more central aspect of the tumour and may impart a gold appearance to the tumour grossly on cut section.
Aldosterone-secreting adrenal cortical adenomas often have lipid-rich clear cells centrally, with compact cells and zona glomerulosa–type cells at the peripheral aspect of the lesion.

This aldosterone-secreting adrenal cortical adenoma is composed almost entirely of cells that resemble the zona glomerulosa. However, aldosterone-secreting adrenal cortical adenomas can have a heterogeneous appearance with many different cell types.

Although nesting is a very common architectural pattern in aldosterone-secreting adenomas, a variety of patterns can be seen. This lesion has a very prominent pattern of growth of linear cords of cells.
This aldosterone-producing adrenal cortical adenoma has a pseudoglandular growth pattern. A variety of patterns and mixtures of patterns can be seen in adrenal cortical adenomas.
This aldosterone-producing adrenal cortical adenoma has prominent areas of glandular-like growth.
A 23 mm aldosterone-producing adrenal cortical adenoma. The golden-yellow colour reflects the high lipid content.
This photograph shows a 40 mm cortisol-producing adrenal cortical adenoma.
A non-functioning clear cell–rich adenoma is shown.

diagnosis: Non-tumorous cortical atrophy in Cushing syndrome
legend: The non-tumorous adrenal cortex shows atrophy in patients with cortisol-producing adrenal cortical neoplasms. The cortical atrophy is characterized by a thin adrenal cortex (often < 2 mm) and an absent or significantly reduced zona reticularis.

Aldosterone-producing adrenal cortical carcinoma and adenoma are solitary lesions clearly visible by both routine H&E and immunohistochemical staining for CYP11B2 (aldosterone synthase). Smaller (subcentimetre) solitary lesions visible by H&E and immunohistochemistry (IHC) are designated as aldosterone-producing nodules (APNs), whereas their counterparts that may be hard to distinguish using H&E but are always visualized on IHC are called aldosterone-producing micronodules (APMs; formerly known as aldosterone-producing cell clusters). When multifocal, these entities are termed multiple APN and multiple APM, respectively (formerly known as micronodular hyperplasia). Aldosterone-producing diffuse hyperplasia is characterized by continuous CYP11B2 staining along the zona glomerulosa.
